The Recorded Sayings of Master Mu’an Kang upon his First Residence at Dàfàn Chán Monastery on Mount Mingyán, Tiantai;
Compiled by His Dharma Heirs Qingyi and Others of Guangxiao Chán Monastery in Huangyan, Taizhou Prefecture.
On the sixth day of the twelfth month in the year of Zhìzhèng Dingyou, the Master entered the monastery. Pointing to the mountain gate, he said: “A thousand...”
Many people pushing against a door is not as good as one person pulling the bolt. Then, beckoning with his hand, he said:
"All the people of the great earth enter through this very place. He let out a shout.
The Patriarch’s Hall: iron beaks and tongues of steel; river-like eyes and sea-like mouths. The elephant king turns in a circle; the lion roars.
Occupying this room, all the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past have driven their stakes and rowed their oars right here. Do you wish now to see the New Ming Cliff?
He raises his staff, strikes it down, and says: "When the dragon-sleeve is swept aside, the whole body is revealed—the place where the elephant king walks."
Cutting off the tracks of the foxes, he took up the temple notice and said: "Ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion great oceans, and ten billion suns and moons—all are contained within this.
The precious seal is wondrous in the void; layer upon layer, the brocade seams unfold."
Preface to the Mountain Gate: Eye meets eye; mind knows mind. If human sentiments are harmonious, one grows stout even by drinking water.

Preface to the Rivers and Lakes: Mountains are long and waters are vast; the moon is the breast and the wind is the lapel. Not separated by so much as a hair’s breadth, they illuminate the past and soar through the present.
Commentary on the Various Mountains. At Tiantai in the Four Ming Mountains, brilliance joins with lush greenery. A single phrase is fully raised; for a thousand ages there has been no peer.
Pointing to the Dharma seat, he said: "The entire earth is this precious Lotus King Throne. When walking, I walk together with all of you."

When seated, he sat together with the assembly. Looking around at those to his left and right, he said, "Because of walking, one swings the arms. Having ascended another level, he finally took his place upon the seat.
Holding up the incense, he said: "This incense is most supreme and most precious; it penetrates the past and permeates the present. I burn it here in this precious burner."
I respectfully offer these prayers for the longevity of the present Emperor—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! May he be as bright as the sun and moon;

may his life span be equal to that of heaven and earth! Next, he takes up the incense and says: "This incense is such that empty space cannot contain it and the great earth cannot support it. East of Zhejiang, West..."
Throughout the province, he traveled from place to place, seeking to buy high and sell low, yet in the end, not a single person would pay his price.
He lingered at Mount Wanshou until he encountered an old, witless "frozen pus-bag," who cast him aside into a heap of refuse.
For twenty years, he was truly beyond the reach of even a spoon. Today, picking him up with a casual hand, I offer him as the former abbot of Kaifu.
Later, he resided at Lingyan, the fifth generation of Songyuan. Master Lia’an Yu burned it all away in a single incense burner;

he did not seek to repay his teacher’s virtue or commemorate his thoughts, but rather desired to have his influence pervade heaven and earth. He then inserted an incense stick, called upon the assembly, and as they raised their heads, he said:

"I have struck your nostrils and burned out your eyes. Thereupon, he sat in the lotus position. Master Hanyan struck the gavel and said: [The text continues with the formal proceedings of the ordination.]
"O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary truth.
The Master spoke these words: "The primary truth is as bright as the radiant sun and as vast as the great void; awaken to it directly and immediately."

He roams freely throughout the world. Should this not yet be so, I ask that you question me regarding any doubts. At that time, a monk stepped forth from the assembly and said: "Shide and Hanshan’s ancient site of enlightenment:
the true body of the Vajra is revealed in its majestic grandeur. High-lifting the precious seal, vast as heaven and earth—may it be proclaimed at every shrine and in every speck of dust.
For the sake of the nation, he opens the hall; we pray that the Master will offer blessings for the Emperor. He replied: "The heavens drape a jeweled canopy."
The mountains and rivers are still; golden lotuses spring from the earth, and the sun and moon are ever new.

The student said, "If this is so, then all living beings receive the Emperor’s power, and the four seas delight in plowing and sowing. The Master replied, "The Purple Palace opens wide, and the monument to the realm of longevity stands firm.

The student said, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the prayers for the Emperor; as for the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, what is it like? The Master replied, "Three before, three after."

The student asked: "In the past, when Baoshou opened the hall for teaching, Sansheng pushed forward a monk, and Baoshou immediately struck him. What was the meaning of this? He replied: "It was like striking a golden bell atop Mount Sumeru. The student asked: "Sansheng said, 'If you act as a teacher in such a manner, you will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou,' and Baoshou threw down his staff and returned to his quarters. What does this mean? He replied: "It was like a great thunderclap following a flash of lightning. The student asked: "Why did he return to his quarters? He replied: "Because there was no one left to strike. The student asked: "Was it not because there was no one to receive the blow? He replied: "It was because there was no one to receive the blow. "Venerable sir, how is it? The monk replied, "An ox-hide drumhead covers the pillar. The monk bowed. The Master then said: "The World-Honored One held up a flower;
Kāśyapa smiled. Bodhidharma faced the wall; the Second Patriarch sought peace of mind. When the tiger roars, the wind arises; when the dragon cries, the mist rises.
Wisdom cannot fathom it; consciousness cannot know it. Therefore, though one exhausts all profound dialectics, it is like a single hair..."
Placed within the great void, exhausting the pivotal mechanisms of the world, it is like a single drop cast into a vast abyss.

Transcending both the mundane and the sagely, it encompasses the past and enshrouds the present, until heaven and earth are vast and open, the sun and moon shine brightly, and the myriad realms become a secure and bounded domain.
The four seas rejoice in the transformation of non-action. Holding up the staff and striking it once, he says: "One sees only the imperial wind forming a single expanse;
one knows not where the boundaries lie."
Again, it is raised: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
The monk said, "Master, do not point to external objects to show people. Zhaozhou said, "I am not pointing to external objects to show you. The monk said...
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.

The Master remarked, "Zhaozhou was forged from refined steel and cast from raw iron; yet when examined closely, he has not yet forgotten the realm of objective phenomena—he is covered head to toe in mud and water.
If someone were to ask Mingyan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? I would simply say to him: "Layered cliffs rising high above the azure heavens."
[The Master] said: "Externally, it overwhelms the myriad peaks of Mount Sumeru.
That evening, during a small *sengcan* (informal sermon), a monk came forward and asked: "When Deshan held a small *sengcan*, why did he not answer the question?
The Master said: "The Emperor’s decree within the realm; the General’s command beyond the borders. The monk asked: "When Zhaozhou held a small *sengcan*, why did he, however, answer the question?"
The Master said, "A mad dog runs through the imperial pardon; the feudal lords clear the way. A monk bowed, and the Master said, "Mingyan has been seen through by you.
He then said: "The Buddhas did not appear in the world; the Patriarchs did not come from the West. The gate of liberation stands open, penetrating in all directions.
Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. Water flows to the damp; fire seeks the dry. Each and every one covers heaven and earth."
Everywhere there is the resonant sound of jade and metal. Maidservants employ Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; handmaidens regard Śākyamuni and Maitreya.
They drive the oxen of the plowmen, causing the crops of others to flourish; they seize the food of the hungry, teaching them to forever end their hunger and emptiness.
One may call this the wondrous function of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); one may also call it the suchness of the natural order (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the Master Hanshan said:
Hanshan’s Untainted Cliff: this cliff is most essential for salvation. Unmoved by the winds of the eight worldly concerns, it has been transmitted as a marvel by people of ten thousand ages.
Do you all know where its true location lies? When the shadows of white clouds disperse, the green mountains emerge; from the secluded rocks and lofty cliffs, the precious moon is full.
Again, he raised the case: When Mazu appeared in the world, Nanyue sent a monk to ask him, "What is it?

Mazu said, "Since the time of chaos, for thirty years, salt and sauce have not been lacking. The Master said: "He opened wide the eastern gate, allowing the patch-robed monks of the world to return satiated;
this was only possible because of that old man Mazu. As for the single upper orifice of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one has not yet seen even a dream of it."
[He] stands. Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he descends from the seat.
On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, he ascends the hall. For six years in the Snowy Mountains, he sat in cold stillness; yet he went forth to bathe in the Nairañjanā River.

At midnight, suddenly beholding the morning star, he did not realize he had struck out his own brain. This has brought misfortune upon the descendants of later generations, each and every one of them falling into pits and ravines.
Qianmingyan’s Separate Path for Provisions: One must meet with the Old Śākyamuni. Holding up his staff, he said:
"A man of true character possesses the will to pierce the heavens; he does not walk where the Tathāgata has walked."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When body and mind are pure, all objects are pure; when all objects are pure, body and mind are pure.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the 'Single Tune of Yunmen'? Yunmen said, "The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month.
Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Profound Prajñāpāramitā. He struck his staff once and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall on the first day of the year, Mingjiao said, "On New Year's Day there is Buddha-dharma. Jingqing said, "On New Year's Day there is no Buddha-dharma.
A-he-he! The spring mountains layer upon layer of chaotic green; the spring waters ripple with empty azure. Vast and silent between heaven and earth.
Standing alone, what limit can one’s gaze reach? (He lets out a shout.
On the Lantern Festival, he ascends the hall to express his gratitude to the two classes of assembly: "One lamp burns; hundreds of thousands of millions of lamps burn together.

It reaches the point where heaven and earth are illuminated through and through, and the Shaoshi Peak increases its brilliance. Those who are long possess the long Dharma-body; those who are short possess the short Dharma-body. North and South."
"East and west, each is restored to its former place. Good assembly, there is no need to pass through the diamond circle, nor is there any need to swallow the thorny *kṣīrikā* fruit.
Then, joining his palms, he said: "The three virtues and six flavors are offered to the Buddha and the Sangha; may all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm partake equally in this offering.
After a long pause, he said: "Where the Golden Immortal walks, every step is a red lotus."
Ascending the hall, he said: "My mind is like the autumn moon; its light shines brightly upon the azure pool.
There is nothing with which it can be compared—how am I to describe it? Namo Siddhārthabhadra! The spring breeze blows through the myriad things, and everywhere flowers bloom."
At the Buddha’s Nirvana Hall, the Master raised an anecdote: A monk asked Dàlóng, “What is the pure Dharma-body?
Dàlóng replied, “Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; stream water is as clear as indigo. The Master said, “Great as Dàlóng was, he only managed to pass through the barrier of birth and death.”
The gate of nirvana has not yet been penetrated. If you wish to understand the pure dharmakāya, it is a hundred thousand and eight thousand [miles away].
Suddenly he picks up his staff and says: "Strike the golden bell! Roll the iron drum! The water flows east; the sun goes west. He leans on the staff and descends from the seat.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the phrase that settles heaven and earth?
The Master said, "The eyebrows swallow the universe; the nostrils obstruct Mount Sumeru. The monk asked, "What is the phrase that follows the waves and drifts with the current?

The Master said, "The golden-haired lion tramples the foxes' den; red and white flowers bloom everywhere in the spring breeze. The monk asked, "What is the phrase that cuts off [all flow]? The Master said... [text fragment ends].
The Master said, "The tongue pressed against the upper palate. The monk said, "Today Prince Siddhārtha has descended into birth.
[The Master] asked, "Tell me, is this within the three phrases or outside the three phrases? The Master said, "A Stone Ganda at the crossroads. The monk bowed.
The Master then said, "Riding a white elephant, descending into the royal palace—how thoroughly he sells his own loftiness! Pointing to heaven and earth, he took seven steps."

A wind of elegance that penetrates to the very marrow. Holding up his staff, he said: "Under the bright sun and clear sky, clouds rise and mists surge; the nine dragons spout water to bathe the golden chariot.
For ten thousand generations, it remains lively and agile. He struck the ground with his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall after leaving the hospital, the Master said: "The ancient worthies said, 'Going, going—yet truly not going; coming, coming—yet truly not coming.
I, this mountain monk, do not understand at all; the pillar laughs heartily. To speak thus is like a thoroughly muddled fellow.
When I come, I certainly come; when I go, I certainly go. What is there to understand or not understand? After a long silence, he said: "The Pillar..."
The Master laughed heartily. "The true eye of heaven and earth is opened; the green mountains are beautiful everywhere—step by step, there are pavilions and terraces.
He took up his staff, struck it three times, and descended from the seat.
Record of the Master’s Teachings while Residing at Longhua Baocheng Chan Monastery in Hangzhou, compiled by his disciples Zhìbiàn and others.

On the first day of the ninth month in the year of Jǐchén (1364) of the Zhìzhèng era, the Master entered the monastery. Holding up the official letter of appointment (*zhàfù*), he addressed the assembly, saying:
This is the Great Marshal, the Grand Chancellor. It is the official verification that proclaims the true nostrils of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from antiquity.
Do you all understand? His body spans the universe; with a single phrase, he settles the fundamental tenets.
Pointing to the Dharma seat, he took a step and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru; with feet crossed, he sat upon the Bodhi seat. Ten thousand virtues do not bring him here;
he completely transcends the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya.

Having ascended the seat and finished the incense offering in honor of the Emperor, he next held up the incense and said: "When this incense is picked up, heaven turns and earth revolves; when it is set down, the rains fall in accordance with the seasons."

The wind was calm. For the sake of the Thousand Buddhas Pagoda Cloister and Master Yuyang of the South Hall, he burned incense in a single burner—not seeking to repay virtue or requite kindness, but solely to perfume their nostrils.
He then sat in the lotus posture. Master Lingyin struck the gavel and said:
"You assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary truth.
The Master spoke these words: "The primary truth has never increased among the Buddhas, nor has it ever decreased among sentient beings."
With a single blow, it was shattered; its radiance spread throughout the entire realm. Was there no one among the assembly who could step forward to join in the proclamation?
A monk asked: "The three assemblies of the Dragon Flower open wide, reaching to the heavens; the lamp-stand and the lantern smile with cheeks full of joy.
Not only do they manifest as hundreds of billions of transformation bodies, but from every dust mote, jade towers emerge. What is the Master’s way of acting for the sake of others?"
[The Master] said: "Above the head, vast and boundless; beneath the feet, vast and boundless. The monk said: "If that is so, then the whole earth and all under heaven are universally enlightened;
every person has their state settled and their country at peace. The Master said: "On the top of the ten-thousand-year-old pine, the peach of immortality forms.
A monk asked: "What was the meaning of Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall? The Master said: "Oil-frying a stone pillar base. The monk prostrated.
[The student] bows. The Master says, "There is no place for you to open your mouth. He then says: "This very mind, mind, mind is Buddha.
It is the most wondrous thing in the worlds of the ten directions. Its transverse and vertical marvelous functions are truly pitiable; nothing else compares to the reality of this mind.
He raises his whisk and says, "Potalaka (Bagu Daiheshang) has arrived! How do you do? How do you do? I took you for Potalaka..."
Furthermore, it turns out that the Great Being Shanhui of the Double-Trees Grove is, at this very moment, atop the tip of the whisk, emitting great radiance and reciting these wondrous verses:
"Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; Morning after morning, one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, we are always in each other's company;
In speech or silence, we dwell together. Not even a hair’s breadth separates us, Like a shadow following its form. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes..."
"Right here—this very sound of my voice is it. Good assembly! In every place, light shines brilliantly; in every place, one attains great mastery.
It is so in every atom, so in every world-system, so in every thought-moment. Truly, the imperial wind fans far and wide, and the Buddha-sun hangs high in the sky.
May all beings among gods and humans alike receive benefit and joy. [He raises his staff and strikes once, saying: "The four seas are clear and still."
The Pure Heaven is unified; arms and shields are laid aside as they celebrate peace.
Again, a monk asked National Teacher Nanyue Rang: "When a mirror is used to cast an image, once the image has been formed, why does it no longer reflect?
Nanyue said, "Although it no longer reflects, it cannot deceive him by even a single point. The Master said, "The old..."
Nanyue held up the single stroke prior to when sentient beings and Buddhas were yet unformed—a matter that startles heaven and shakes earth, penetrating the ancient and encompassing the present.
"Have any of you ever seen it even in a dream? After a long silence, he said: "Cloudless, clouds arise upon the ridge; the moon exists, falling into the heart of the waves.
He then descended from his seat.
Incense Offering on the Anniversary of the First Patriarch: I originally came to this land, a majestic tiger with horns upon its head.

Transmitting the Dharma to save deluded beings, he shattered the city of Caizhou. One flower blooms into five petals; the sun and moon shine with brilliant radiance. The fruition is naturally accomplished.
The green water reflects the blue mountains. Do you see the Great Master Bodhidharma? His realization of the Great Way transcends all measure; his penetration of the Buddha-mind exceeds all limits.
He is not entangled with ordinary beings or sages; he is called a Patriarch because he is utterly transcendent. (He then inserts incense.)
Ascending the hall, the Master raised up the words of Panshan: "The one path leading upward—thousand sages have not transmitted it. He then cited Ciming:

"The one path leading upward—thousand sages do not so [attain it]. The Master said, "When these two great elders speak in this manner, they are very much like joining bamboo poles to point at the moon."
The Way of the Dragon Flower; the single path leading upward, pervading the earth and pervading the heavens.
Entering the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No. The Master said:
The dog has no Buddha-nature. Head straight, tail straight. Leaping out beyond the upper barrier. Swift as a command. *Chan*.
On the occasion of the Buddha’s Birth, the Master ascended the hall and, with his whisk, made the gesture of ladling soup: "I now bathe all the Tathāgatas. Pure..."
This is a treasury of merit adorned with wisdom. It causes sentient beings of the five turbidities to leave behind defilement and together realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Good assembly, if this is so, then every mote of dust is the Buddha; every land is the Buddha; every day is bathing the Buddha;
and every moment is bathing the Buddha. Have you all ever attained such realization? If you have realized it, I would not dare to slight you.
"If you do not realize it, all of you shall surely become Buddhas. [The Master] threw down his whisk, performed a dance, and descended from his seat.
One day, a monk asked, "What was it like before Oxhead saw the Fourth Patriarch? The Master said, "A cangue upon his head and shackles upon his feet.
The monk asked, "What was it like after he saw him? The Master said, "If he wishes to sit, he sits; if he wishes to walk, he walks."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: Once, a seer with five supernatural powers asked the World-Honored One, "The Buddha possesses six supernatural powers, while I possess only five.
What is that one power? The World-Honored One called out to the seer, and the seer responded. The World-Honored One said, "That one power—ask me about it.
The verse says: "That one power—ask me about it. On the head of the Huangbo tree hang honeyed fruits. The lantern..."
Clapping hands with a laugh: the auspicious qilin snaps its golden chains.

Entering the hall, he raised the case: "Prince Nalakuvara dismembered his flesh to return it to his mother and dismembered his bones to return them to his father; only then did he manifest his true body."

Exercising great supernormal power, he preached the Dharma for his parents. Master Foyan Yuan said: "Since the flesh has returned to the mother and the bones have returned to the father, after all, what is used as the body?
Tell me, what Dharma was preached? He spoke in verse: "Flesh and bone are both returned to the parents;
Throughout the oceans of lands in the ten directions, the whole body is revealed. The clouds part and the wild waters float green across the sky; The rain..."
Passing through the spring mountains, their dark green hues appear freshly washed.
This is the record of the discourse at Jinshan Longyou Chan Temple in Zhenjiang.
Compiled by the tonsured disciples Baori and others.
On the twenty-first day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Hongwu era of the Great Ming, the Master entered the temple. Pointing to the mountain gate, he said:
"One gate is all gates; one entry is all entries. The blue sky and white rain fly; the great ocean and Mount Sumeru stand firm."
He lets out a shout. The Buddha Hall Master says: "Brick tiles and rubble; jade towers and jeweled palaces. Upon the tips of the hundred grasses is the sixteen-foot golden body.
After a long silence, he says: "Look out beyond the heavens—'Who is there like me?'"
At the Hall of the Monastery, he said: "From where does the numinous come? From where does the sage arise?
Jade emerges from Mount Kunlun; gold is produced in Li-water. At the Hall of the Patriarchs, he said: "It is thus in the Western Heaven; it is thus in this Eastern Land.
All the old monks of the world are thus; I, the old monk, am also thus. Inserting the incense, he said: "Sealed by a single seal, it is impervious to leakage."
Sitting in his room, Śākyamuni at Vulture Peak merely obtained one peg; facing the wall at Shaolin, Bodhidharma merely obtained one peg.
Holding up his staff and pressing it against his knee, he said: "Horizontal, it is up to me; vertical, it is up to me; giving, it is up to me; taking away, it is up to me."
He then struck the desk once and said: "Water flows to what is moist; fire seeks what is dry.

The Prefectural Administration’s inscription states: "His station anchors the mountains and rivers; neither lenient nor fierce, yet he stands but a few inches from the Nine Heavens, his radiance shining resplendent."

Pointing to the Dharma seat, he said: "The precious seat of the emptiness of dharmas—how high or how low? Sitting upon it, one cuts off all manifold distinctions; the direct path is open. A thatched hut replaces the lapis lazuli tiles.
He then ascended the seat and held up the incense, saying: "This incense encompasses heaven and earth, serving as both canopy and pedestal.
It nurtures the great trichiliocosm, its fragrance benefiting the ten directions. I burn this toward the precious burner specifically to offer prayers for the long life of the Emperor."
May the Greatly Enlightened Ruler of the World, the present Emperor, enjoy ten thousand years of auspicious life—ten thousand, ten thousand, ten thousand times ten thousand years!

May the Empress live as long as Heaven and Earth; may the Crown Prince live for a thousand autumns. Furthermore, may all those of celestial rank within the imperial palace likewise be blessed. We humbly pray that Heaven and Earth share his longevity, and the sun and moon shine with equal brilliance.
May he govern by the Golden Wheel so that seas and mountains are at peace, and may the Jade Candle be harmonized so that the movements of Heaven follow their proper order.
Again, he lifts the incense and says: "This incense is pure and firm both within and without; it is gazed upon from near and afar.

We offer it for all officials, great and small, of the entire prefecture and the entire district, and for those who guard and protect them, so that their fortunes and lifespans may increase together. We humbly pray:"
His administrative achievements surpass those of the Han and Tang dynasties; his name shines upon bamboo and silk.
Next, he holds up the incense and says: "This incense, spanning from antiquity to the present, is neither subtle nor coarse.
For the third time it is brought forth to be offered to my successor in the lineage of Vajradhvaja, the Great Abbot Lia’an of Qianfo Ciyun Monastery. One burner is now ignited."
[He] withdrew. To repay the grace of the Dharma-milk, he sat cross-legged and uttered these words:
"The bell does not ring without being struck; the drum does not sound without being beaten.

Is there anyone here, a master of the ultimate path, who will come forth to stir up the discussion? (The questions and answers are not recorded). The summary states: "The World-Honored One has secret words."
Filling the three thousandfold world system, Kāśyapa does not conceal it. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth radiate light;
it is not the mind, not the Buddha, and not a thing.
By this, Your Majesty opens up the myriad states and widely proclaims the sacred transformation. By this, the Chancellor harmonizes the nine realms and regulates the Yin and Yang.
By this, the Six Armies sweep away the calamities of the heavens, and by this, the hundred officials propagate the administration of government.
Religion thereby assists and supports the royal way; through it, the people and all things find a firm foundation for their livelihood.
The wind of Yao spreads everywhere, and the sun of Shun hangs high in the heavens. Then one sees sweet dew descend and divine birds arrive; auspicious wheat grows, and the *qiche* (ox-cart) emerges.
At such a time, tell me, how would you offer your prayers? Striking the whisk, he said: "The heavens are high and the myriad forms are upright; the seas are vast..."
The hundred rivers flow toward the sea;

once again, it is raised. Attendant Wang visited Linji. As Linji was leading the Attendant on a casual stroll within the Sangha Hall, the Attendant asked, "Do the monks in this hall study the sutras? Linji replied, "They do not study the sutras. The Attendant asked again.

The attendant asked, "Do you still practice seated meditation? Linji said, "I do not practice seated meditation. The attendant asked, "Since you neither read the sutras nor practice seated meditation, what exactly are you doing?
Linji said, "I am simply teaching everyone to become a Buddha and an ancestral patriarch. The attendant [was thus enlightened].
Dawu said, "Though gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract. The Master said, "Old Linji held high the Seal of Orthodoxy.

When Wang, the Attendant, directly accepted it in its very essence, he casually beheld the radiance of the Patriarchs' Way; the royal order was made manifest and clear. Assembly, do you all understand?
He flings open the locks of the golden hall and strikes the bell of the jade tower. He descended from his seat.
That evening, during the informal discourse (*xiaochan*), he said: "In antiquity, the informal discourse was called 'family instruction. What is meant by 'family'?

It refers to the family of worldly convention, the family of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and the family of the three realms (*tridhātu*). Because one is able to leave them and not re-enter them, it is called 'family instruction. We, however, have abandoned our biological parents."
Wearing robes of discolored hue, not entangled in worldly conditions, dwelling peacefully in forests and wilds—this is called "leaving the home of the mundane world.
Realizing the nature of both defiled and pure phenomena, not lingering in the toil of dust and labor, and not adhering to deluded attachments—this is called "leaving the home of the five aggregates.

Riding upon sound and traversing form, transcending the sages and surpassing the ordinary, shattering empty space and attaining great sovereignty—this is called "leaving the home of the three realms. If one can indeed act in this way...
It is so. According to their merit, rewards are bestowed: fields, houses, clothing, and various precious jewels. This old monk does not scatter or begrudge them;
he treats them as if they were the bright pearl within his topknot, handing them over with both hands. Will the great assembly approve? [He raises his staff and strikes it once.
"The Sea God knows its value but not its price; it is left for the human world to illuminate the night."

Fadeng said, "It is you who bring calamity upon me. The Master said, "Great Dharma-deng! You are truly wide awake in your dreams, speaking of bringing calamity upon me and bringing calamity upon you.
When will you ever attain a state that is pure, unencumbered, and thoroughly clean?

New Jinshan shall also make one move: take advantage of the fine weather to finish roofing the house; seize the moment to reap the grain; pay the taxes and royal tribute; and then beat your belly with contentment."
Sing a high song. Descend from the seat.
Two groups of monks remain to ascend the hall. A single tree does not form a forest; a single strand does not form a thread.
Amidst a grove of sandalwood, there must be sandalwood surrounding it; within a lion’s den, a lion must be permitted to roar. Together we shall erect the Dharma banner and join in [the practice].

Establishing the fundamental tenet, one is able to wash the Buddha-sun with light and spread the profound breeze. It benefits the world and nourishes the people, so that each may settle their own household affairs.
It is like hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room; the lights shine upon one another, yet each does not borrow from the other.
Thus it is said: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. At such a time, tell me: how can one avoid being wounded?

Regarding the single phrase "the meaning of things," how can it be brought forth? "The numinous earth has mountain snow and grass at every step; the Sangha-treasure is a pearl from the blue sea for every person. [He] descends from his seat.

On the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascends the hall to express his gratitude to the Head Seat, the Abbot’s Assistant, the Administrative Officers, and the Venerable Elders. "Cutting through jade, floating gǔpú; wrapped..."
Piles of gold and glutinous millet—once sated, one forgets a hundred hungers. A single phrase transcends all suffering. The fragrant breeze blows from the south;

it sweeps softly across the courtyard and doors. When human relations are harmonious and cordial, responses ring out like bells and drums. Red mouths and white tongues are transformed into fine songs and dances.
Resplendent is the Shaolin lineage; majestic is the Patriarch who faced the wall. A monk asked: "What is this 'facing the wall'?"
The message from the Patriarch on the Wall says: "It is not right to interfere with Nanquan’s bowl-position;
it is not right to turn over the entire Great Canon; it is not right to pass through the golden circle or swallow the chestnut thorn. After all, how is it?
"Go drink tea."
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Mañjuśrī spending the summer retreats in three places.

When Kāśyapa struck the gavel, intending to expel Mañjuśrī, suddenly hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs were seen spreading out to his left and right. The World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you wish to expel?"
The Master said: "Mañjuśrī is eight-sided and translucent; Kāśyapa is of one flavor and carries a wooden board.
Within carrying the board lies the message of translucence; within translucence lies the pattern of carrying the board. Since both are beyond involvement, how is it ultimately?
Facing the pestle, facing the mortar; planting crabapples at the bottom of the well. This year’s peach and plum are precious—one fruit is worth a thousand pieces of gold. Below.
[The Master] sat.

One day he gave a teaching by means of a *chuyǔ* (a hanging word), saying: "How much distance is there between that which was before King Vairocana and your daily activities as they currently manifest?
He further said: "If one were to smash the skull open, where would you see Old Śākyamuni? He also said: "When [the Buddha] came..."
For what reason is he without a mouth?

Holding the whisk at Tianning Monastery in Qinchuan for the Winter Solstice, he gave this instruction: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it is only in reliance upon conditions that it is born. He then manifested [the following].

Before you, lamps and candles glow brightly, surrounded by elephants and dragons, extending even to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the sun, moon, and stars; the grasses, trees, and forests;
and all people, animals, plants, and weeds—all these are objects. Which among them is the Dharma? It is the lamps and candles glowing brightly.
Surrounded by elephant-dragons, and extending even to the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the sun, moon, and stars; the grasses, trees, and forests;
humans, beasts, and blades of straw—all are entirely the Dharma. Which among these is the "object"?

If you can see this clearly and with distinct clarity, you may then stride across the summit of the highest peak and take wide steps at the bottom of the deepest sea. Is there anyone so swift and brilliant?
"Come forth, you patch-robed monks! Let us sing and respond to one another. A monk asked, "How was it before Bodhidharma had come? The Master replied, "Filling the valleys and filling the ditches.
The monk pressed further, "And how was it after he came? The Master replied, "Illuminating heaven and reflecting the earth.
The monk pressed further, "Ultimately, how was it? The Master replied, "Mount Sumeru and the Fragrant Water Sea. He then said, "With doors and windows wide open, ten thousand miles are not..."
Hanging clouds. Who is it facing the window? Suddenly emerging from the blue sky and the bright sun. Just so, just so:
beating the drum in Jambudvīpa in the south, ascending the hall in Uttarakuru in the north. Not so, not so: rolling red dust at the bottom of the sea.
White waves fly from the mountain peaks; within suchness, there is not-suchness. Blowing an iron flute on the crossroads, one acts with feigned folly atop a thousand peaks.
Within non-suchness, yet it is suchness: at the dead of night, one sings a folk song, pointlessly startling the sleep of Brahmā.
With the nine heavens free of obscuration, what need is there for penetration? A single ray of divine light has never been absent.
Obscure and dim. [The Master] picks up his staff and says, "Look! Look! This staff here transforms into Śākyamuni Buddha, emitting a great radiance that illuminates the trichiliocosm.
Above it reaches the pinnacle of existence; below it penetrates the golden wheel.
Within this space, he expounds the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, for it is without duality, without division, without distinction, and without interruption."

Just as Vairocana Tathāgata transforms into a pavilion of wondrous jewels, and the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna emerges from a seven-storied tower of exquisite gems, they praise and congratulate one another, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Rare, rare!
At that very moment, the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, unable to restrain his joy, leaps for gladness, stirs the auspicious winds, and pours down the nectar of immortality.
[The Master] gave a shout. Then, turning toward the assembly on Vulture Peak, he addressed the great multitude, saying: "The mass of yin has been stripped away; the first yang has already arisen.
The movement of the celestial dial shifts; the winter solstice arrives. May you receive blessings in accordance with the season; there is nothing that does not bring joy.
We broaden the auspicious offerings of ten thousand ages and unify the harmonious vital energy. He struck his staff once and said: "The waters return to the great ocean, and the waves subside."
Zhuang: "Clouds reach Cangwu; the atmosphere is lofty.

He raised it again: Once, while at Dongshan, during the winter night while eating fruit, he asked Chief Seat Tai, "There is a thing, black as lacquer, which reaches up to support the heavens and down to buttress the earth.
It is always present within the midst of activity, yet it cannot be contained within the midst of activity. Where does its fault lie?"
"Where was the fault? Tai said, "The fault lay in the act of movement. Dongshan ordered his attendant to remove the fruit table.
The Master said, "Dongshan laid his plans within the tent; Head Seat Tai won the victory a thousand miles away, whereby inner and outer harmony were achieved."
Above and below are as one. Nevertheless, consider this: when Dongshan ordered his attendant to remove the fruit table, what was his intention?
To overturn the seas and mountains in search of a true friend; to stir the heavens and earth to behold Great Peace.

At Lingyin Monastery on the winter solstice, while holding the whisk, he gave this instruction: "The ultimate point above is like the sky universally covering, like the earth universally supporting, like the sun universally shining, like the wind universally blowing, and like a great mass of fire; to approach it is to have one's face scorched."
"It is like a drum smeared with poison: to strike it is to lose one's body and life. Is there no monk among this assembly who does not cherish his own life?

Come forth and let us challenge and inspire one another! At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "Blowing the great Dharma conch, beating the great Dharma drum, expounding the great Dharma meaning, raining down the great Dharma rain—at such a moment as this, we pray to hear the essential teaching. [The Master] replied:
[The Master] said: "The whale swallows the seawater until it is exhausted, revealing the coral branches. [The Disciple] asked: "What is the blowing of the great Dharma conch?
[The Master] replied: "A single sound pervades the ears of all people. [The Disciple] asked: "What is the beating of the great Dharma drum? [The Master] replied:
Heaven shook and the earth trembled. The student asked, "What is the great meaning of expounding the Dharma? He replied, "A single character does not admit of a stroke.
The student asked, "What is the raining down of the great Dharma rain? He replied, "The three types of grass and two types of trees sprout simultaneously.
The student asked, "Splitting open Mount Tai, the thunder is not yet fierce; illuminating the vast ocean, the moon is not yet bright. He replied, "A crow that has shed its shell."
The tortoise flew up into the sky; the monk returned to the assembly. He followed this by saying: "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. Then he said:
"If there is even a single dharma, Vairocana falls among the common folk. If there are not even ten thousand dharmas, Samantabhadra loses his realm.
It cannot be thus, nor can it be otherwise. It cannot be both thus and otherwise. It is the wondrous blade."

The sword is constantly manifest before one. Should you even attempt to lift your eyes, it would lay corpses across ten thousand miles. [The Master] takes up his staff, strikes once to the left, saying:
"Within this place, the myriad yin energies are completely stripped away. He strikes once to the right, saying: "Within this place, the single yang energy begins to regenerate.
He then holds the staff horizontally and says: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—the harmonious breath returns in secret; grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—the warm wind [begins to blow]."
Universally fanning the wind, the Buddha Hall vies with the mountain gate for its plaque; the lantern confronts the pillar, raising its brows. Flying Eagle Peak leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens;
West Lake pours into the nostrils of all people. Everywhere the Precious Seal is fully revealed; at every point its majestic authority is displayed.
It is like a golden-winged bird cleaving the sea, straightway seizing and swallowing the dragon; like a fragrant elephant crossing the river.
The river: crossing it by cutting through the current. Again, like a lute made of lion sinew—when struck, all other sounds are instantly silenced.
A-ha-ha! Ra-ra-li! Striking a golden bell atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, taking wide strides upon the seabed of the great ocean.
The barefoot Persian wears a Daoist crown; the wrathful Nātha holds aloft an iron pillar. Leaning on his staff, he says: "I split open Mount Hua!"
Liantian Xiu: "He releases the Yellow River until it is utterly clear.
He raised the case again: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is the matter of winter coming? The worthy said, "The capital produces great yellow myrobalan.
The Master said: "An ancient worthy holding up the matter in this way is just like throwing down a raw iron caltrop on level ground."
I teach you that advancing there is no gate, and retreating there is no path. If you are a swift and keen monk, with a single bite you shall break through it;
then you will see the sweat flow from your entire body, all ailments eliminated, walking alone upon the great earth, free and at ease.
I have composed this verse on the spot to present to the assembly: The Capital produces the Great Purgative, Its high price suppresses all other regions. A single blow cures a hundred ailments.
Shattered [are delusions]; its radiance fills the Great Tang.
Two gāthās in praise of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.

I prostrate to the vast and pure ocean that nurtures and sustains boundless worlds. Through the faculty of hearing, you reveal the gate of perfect penetration to rescue and protect the multitudes of suffering sentient beings.
The fundamental nature of sentient beings is inherently pure; it is no different from that of Avalokiteśvara.
In a single kṣaṇa, by turning one’s thought, one can realize awakening; with quiescent extinction manifesting before one, one transcends the mundane world. It is like the bright, full moon.

Traveling through empty space, its reflection falls upon all rivers and seas; the light of the moon and the moon itself mutually reflect one another, yet ultimately they do not depart from the original lunar form.
Now that I have made such an observation, the essence of every land and every atom is likewise so.
I universally pray that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may achieve the true meaning of perfect penetration.
What is heard is exhausted by hearing; what is perceived is empty of perception. Seeking out sounds to save those in suffering, you open the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf.
When the single truth is not obscured, every particle of dust is liberated; when the six faculties cease their activity, every dharma is perfectly penetrating.

Throughout the ten directions there are no shadows; within the three realms there are no tracks left behind. Sitting and cutting off heaven and earth in their billions of forms, the golden bird flies forth from the eastern sea-gate.

The Great Being’s Way is characterized by non-action and non-abiding, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating. The essence of all living beings throughout the great earth is fundamentally the same. When purity reaches its ultimate limit, radiant light is the true Mother of Buddhas;
in every speck of dust and every world-system, the profound mystery soars forth.
The Great Being appears as a youth, his topknot bound without curls; he brings spring to the great earth. Reclining askance among the crags, he manifests the natural truth.
Within the realm of universal penetration across the boundless sea of suffering, hearing sounds with one’s own eyes is ever new in every place.
The Great Being utters the lion’s roar;

he speaks with fearlessness. The eye is the treasury, the sinews are the cords; the mouth preserves the tongue. This is the dharma-gate of perfect penetration—a single flake of snow upon a red furnace.
The ultimate *amṛta* is refreshing drop by drop; it universally removes the afflictions and fevers of all sentient beings.

The Great Being with forty-two arms is the Dharma King’s great general, universally bestowing fearlessness. Whether through compassion or majesty, whether through meditative concentration or wisdom, he may manifest as Śakrā.
Rāśu. Eighty-four thousand [hands], or manifesting forty-two arms in the mudrā; above, they accord with the Buddhas of the ten directions in their shared power of compassion;
below, they unite with the sentient beings of the six realms in their shared longing for mercy.

Responding to these two types of seeking without fail or error, they deliver one across the eight difficulties without hindrance or obstruction—what is called "universal penetration throughout the ten directions."
It is truly revealed as inconceivable; it uplifts both sentient and insentient beings, causing them all to enter together into the foremost samādhi of the Vajra King Buddha-Mother.

The Great Being Mañjuśrī, in his guise of one clad in grass garments, dwells in the Vajra Cave, appearing and disappearing at will. At Mount Qingliang, he sports with sovereign ease; in every blade of grass and every tree, he manifests the wondrous Dharmakāya;
in every word and every smile, he reveals the true Dharmadhātu. That son of the Lü clan experienced a divine encounter through spiritual resonance, attaining the state of Puyi.

His body was draped [in robes], and golden script appeared upon his hands; how could this not be what is called the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena, manifesting the fundamental, wondrous light of the Great Samādhi? Alas! How magnificent!
The Layman Vimalakīrti realized that form is empty, persons are empty, names are empty, and dharmas are empty.

Having realized great Bodhi and attained great liberation, he roared like a golden lion to refute the partial and subdue the small, and he sighed in praise of the Great and extolled the Perfect as dragons and elephants trample through the fields. Since there is no abiding basis, what basis can there be?
What gate is this Gate of Non-duality? A meal from the Fragrant Accumulation fills the entirety of Vaiśālī; a room of ten feet square swallows and eclipses heaven and earth.
*Ei!* That superior man is difficult to respond to; the aged Mañjuśrī loses his wits and spirit.

The Great Being Jingrong took form within an eagle’s nest; his spirit merged with the Dragon Mound. At times moving and at times still, he dwelt in peaceful meditation. Appearing and disappearing as occasion required, he awakened both kings and ministers.
His alms-bowl staff rose upward, manifesting swords, rulers, and fly-whisks; within its mirror-like surface appeared the eras of Qi, Liang, and Chen.
Praising the Mahāyāna: there are words that scatter the chaff and words that are silent. This is divided into fourteen sections; this is the true rejection of the false. There is no path to birth;
one penetrates the ocean of lands throughout the ten directions. It is the food of Nirvāṇa, which satiates the devas and humans of the three realms.

Every single thing fully manifests the sacred form; in every speck of dust, the Wheel of Dharma constantly turns. Where lamps, fire, and incense smoke intermingle, heaven and earth are illuminated by the sun.
The moon becomes ever more radiant and fresh.

The image of Vajra-vikṛta (Huiji) is a transformation of Śākyamuni, the emanation of Vairocana; the light of the precious flower pedestal blazes brilliantly. Śākyamuni manifests his form as Vajra-vikṛta. Behold!

The subcontinents bow down before the demonic and heterodox; every thing is pure and true, and every head manifests both the Exoteric and Esoteric. With great compassion, he offers the nine-fold refined nectar;
with great wrath, he douses them with the elixir of ambrosia. Forging the sages and melting the ordinary, his wondrous function is the total manifestation of his power.
He brought great benefit to both the mundane and supramundane realms, extensively establishing meritorious achievements before and after the Buddhas.
As for the Wayman who planted pine trees at the head of the Turzhang River, within the Shuangfeng Monastery— through successive incarnations, falling once and rising again— he cast down his mattock.
The pines grow tall of their own accord; heaven, earth, and the great world provide shade and coolness.
Borrowing these rhymes to instruct Attendant Bian:
do not take offense that my eyes resemble my eyebrows. For nine years facing the wall—that was my teacher. If you wish to know what existed before your parents were born—
Verse: Remember that time of harsh abuse in the mountain crags;

Gautama employed a hundred stratagems to entice Nanda. With his guts turned upside down and his bowels emptied, there was nothing he could do. Pressed against the gateway of his face, he personally grasped it;
the mute child clapped his hands and suddenly began to sing.
To Master Yunjung Seonjong at Samhak Rock:
The nature of the body is inherently perfect; A hundred thousand suns and moons hang suspended in the void. Whether observing or violating the precepts, all is pure;
One does not fail the transmission of Upāli’s five divisions.
The cowherd boy releases the water-buffalo of Mt. Tui; Warm clouds gather and disperse south and north of the stream. In the spring breeze, the fine grass stretches green to the heavens;
With no rope on its snout, it rests content when full.
At the spot where the箍 (stave) of Master Xian’s bucket exploded, the skull became dry. The three thousandfold world-system of the Buddha-fields is viewed upon the palm of one’s hand.
Blowing forth the unperforated flute for returning home, the sun rises over Fusang, surging from the golden basin.

In the same rhyme, responding to the Chan Master Manzhu’s lines on “Sharing the Same Wind from Three Thousand Li Away”: A pair of eyebrows arches across the eyes; Standing on tiptoe at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, one gazes out.
The wooden man claps his hands as he walks through fire.
An ancient worthy said: "The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness; the dense yellow flowers are none other than Prajñā.
A verse says: "The golden sun shines from the bottom of the sea; the jade horse gallops through the air. Having trampled Mount Sumeru down, one faces south to gaze at the Northern Dipper."

The monk departs as the grass turns green and the flowers turn red; the lion’s roar resounds. Heaven is high and earth is vast as the elephant king strides forth. The wild fox’s skull splits open and the host of demons submits;
once again, we see the Yellow River flow clear for a time.
Holding purity, at the sound of a finger-snap, the door before him opens wide; the pit of excrement transforms into a blue lotus pedestal.
Laughing, he beholds the pure body of Vairocana, rolling out from atop a heap of refuse.
In the same rhyme, I send this to Master Mengtang:
Beholding the mountains and gazing at the waters, he lets go of the *māṇḍala*. How is the fundamental lineage of the Buddhas established? Before the Eight Camphor Peaks, he blows his iron flute;
the wooden man claps his hands and the stone man sings.
I pay homage to the ancestral master Cui Feng Mingjue:
Surging waves strike the shore, the moon is like a basin. On the lakeside dwellings, bamboo reflects upon the gates. Cutting off all streams, there is neither front nor back;
A single, luminous phrase settles heaven and earth.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Mu’an Kang (End). Appendix:
The *Nittō Shū* by Japanese Master Nyōdō states: "In the fourth year of the Eitoku era, the Jiazi year, at the age of sixty."
On the second day of the twelfth month, while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), I went to the memorial service for the Great Dragon Hermitage at Kenneiji.
After the refreshments were finished, I was escorted by Daikyō into Nanyang Hermitage. There, the various elders engaged in miscellaneous conversation.
I asked Chunting about the words I had recently seen in Kangmu Hermitage’s writings, which ended with the phrase "Jiaotai" (郊臺). Chunting said, "When Mu’ān resided at Longhua in Hangzhou..."

It is situated near the Jiaotai (Altar of the Suburbs). Since the Song dynasty moved its capital southward after the Southern Transition, they performed the sacrifice to Heaven at the Southern Suburbs; hence it is called Jiaotai.
This terrace was the altar for the sacrifice to Heaven.
It is further stated: On the twenty-ninth day of the first month in the second year of the Yongde era (the *Renxu* year), the "Discourse on the Ancient Sword" says:

Once, returning from Jiangnan, I encountered six practitioners observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*) at sea. They composed a verse, which says: "The Perfect Enlightenment Monastery is a bubble upon the sea;
The summer retreat and the restraint of the feet are a boat at the river's head. The waxen man knows how to sing the tune of returning home— *Kuannai*! (a cry of joy).
"A single sound, mountains and waters are profound. Once, when he arrived at Kāngmū’s hermitage, he mistakenly recited this verse as a response to a chant, saying, "To call it...
Mū said, "This must be an error; it is not the language of Gujian. The word 'to call' (喚作) is not good... [and so forth].
Mu’an was the dharma successor of Liao’an.
